name: Texas Cloverleaf
description: A heel hook from a reaping position with a unique leg configuration that creates direct rotational pressure on the knee — popularized in no-gi by leg lock specialists.
shortInstruction: Reap the leg, control the far leg, rotate the heel — the Texas Cloverleaf is a heel hook with a unique angle from the reaping position.
summary: The Texas Cloverleaf is a heel hook variation that uses a reaping leg position to attack the knee with direct rotational pressure. The 'cloverleaf' name comes from the way the legs wrap around each other like a four-leaf clover. It is a specialized submission that is most effective from specific leg entanglement configurations and is often used as a surprise attack from positions where the standard heel hook is not available.
whyItWorks: The reaping position creates a unique angle that the standard heel hook does not cover.
The leg configuration traps the opponent's far leg, preventing them from rolling to escape.
It can be entered from positions where the saddle is not available.
Danaher principle: every leg attack should have a chain — the Texas Cloverleaf is the chain from the reap.
commonMistakes: Applying the heel hook before fully establishing the leg entanglement — the reaping position must be secure.
Not controlling their secondary leg — they will spin out.
Using too much rotation too quickly — heel hooks from reaping positions are especially dangerous.
Attempting the Texas Cloverleaf without solid heel hook fundamentals.
coachingCues: Reap deep, control the far leg, rotate safely.
The Texas Cloverleaf is a specialized finish — master the standard heel hook first.
If you can't find the heel, adjust the reaping angle.
safetySummary: The Texas Cloverleaf applies rotational force to the knee — this is a dangerous submission.
Only attempt this submission with trusted training partners who understand leg lock mechanics.
Tap on ANY knee rotational discomfort — do not wait for pain.
Not appropriate for beginners — requires advanced leg lock understanding.
keyCorrections: If you can't find the heel, your reaping angle is too shallow — adjust your leg position.
If they spin out, you lost far leg control — re-establish the secondary leg control.
If they stack you, release and reset — don't fight the stack from this position.

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Leg entanglement: reaping position → control far leg → find the heel → align rotation → apply slow heel hook pressure.

decisionTree.action: The Texas Cloverleaf is an advanced variation — it should only be attempted after mastering the standard inside heel hook.
transition to the standard saddle heel hook.

moneyDetails: The reaping leg should be in a deep reap position — your leg hooks their leg from the inside, crossing the knee line.
Control their far leg by trapping it between your legs or grabbing their ankle.
The heel hook grip is standard: one hand on the heel, one hand on the toes.
Rotate slowly — the finish is about controlled pressure, not speed.
nextStep: After the Texas Cloverleaf, master the standard inside heel hook from the saddle.
fixItFast: Can't find the heel? Adjust your reaping angle.
They spin out? Control their far leg more aggressively.
Feel resistance? Release and re-enter — don't force it.
